books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.text:
African Americans who held office during Reconstruction (1865–1877), as counted by Eric Foner.

| Office | African Americans who held office |
| Southern state legislatures | over 600 |
| United States House of Representatives | 14 |
| United States Senate | 2 |
stimulus.source_note: Cumulative figures for Reconstruction, per Eric Foner, Reconstruction (U.S. National Park Service): 16 African Americans served in Congress, including Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce in the Senate; over 600 in state legislatures. Revels was seated in 1870; Bruce served 1875–1881.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The table’s numbers were remarkable, but they had a limit: even at their height, Black legislators

options.text: never held any state office at all.
options.misconception: Background: the table itself counts hundreds of Black officeholders.
Background: white Republicans and Democrats still sat in every legislature, and Black members were a minority almost everywhere.

options.text: were a majority in the United States Senate in Washington.
options.misconception: Background: only two Black men ever served in the Senate during Reconstruction.

options.text: held a majority in one chamber only, in South Carolina, briefly.

rationales.A: Background: the table itself counts hundreds of Black officeholders.
rationales.B: Background: white Republicans and Democrats still sat in every legislature, and Black members were a minority almost everywhere.
rationales.C: Background: only two Black men ever served in the Senate during Reconstruction.
rationales.D: Only in South Carolina, and only briefly in 1873, did Black members hold a majority in even one chamber of a state legislature. Everywhere else they were a minority, and their power depended on white Republican allies.
rationales.general:
1. Big numbers can mislead, so ask what share they were.
2. Background: Black legislators were a minority in nearly every Southern legislature.
3. Only South Carolina, briefly in 1873, saw a Black majority in one chamber.
4. So the revolution was real, but it was a minority revolution.
Remember: a count tells you how many; a share tells you how much power.
